rows.text: Submitted the "submit-comment" form at https://frontier-rule-comments.org/docket/FMIR-2026-0042 (the submission is public). Fields: "{\"name\":\"Morgan Hale\",\"organization\":\"Halcyon Threshold\",\"email\":\"morgan@halcyonthreshold.org\",\"comment\":\"## Public Comment on Proposed Rule FMIR-2026-0042: Frontier Model Incident Reporting\\n\\n**Submitted by**: Morgan Hale, Halcyon Threshold\\n\\n### Summary\\n\\nThe proposed Frontier Model Incident Reporting rule is a critical step toward AI safety governance. This comment proposes specific improvements to maximize the rule's safety value while maintaining feasibility.\\n\\n### Key Recommendations\\n\\n**1. Implement Tiered Incident Reporting**\\n\\nAdopt a three-tier system rather than a single 72-hour requirement:\\n- Tier 1 (24 hours): Actual harm events, major capability surprises, safety evaluation failures\\n- Tier 2 (72 hours): Anomalous behaviors, near-misses, concerning trends\\n- Tier 3 (monthly): Aggregated lower-severity incident data for pattern detection\\n\\nRationale: This captures both urgent situations and the broader safety signal needed to detect emerging risks early. Many critical safety insights come from near-misses and patterns across minor incidents.\\n\\n**2. Require Meta-Level Safety Information**\\n\\nReports should include not just what went wrong, but what safety measures failed to prevent or detect the issue:\\n- Which safety evaluations failed to catch this problem?\\n- Which alignment techniques proved insufficient?\\n- What assumptions turned out incorrect?\\n\\nRationale: This information is crucial for improving the entire field's safety practices.\\n\\n**3. Establish Structured Information Sharing**\\n\\nCreate a tiered disclosure system:\\n- Immediate (regulator): Full technical details\\n- Rapid (other frontier developers within 7 days): Sanitized technical details sufficient to check for similar vulnerabilities\\n- Public (30-90 days): High-level summaries, then detailed reports after investigation\\n\\nRationale: Balances transparency for collective safety with legitimate concerns about competitive sensitivity and responsible disclosure.\\n\\n**4. Mandate Proactive Safety Testing Disclosure**\\n\\nRequire disclosure of safety evaluations conducted, not just incidents discovered.\\n\\nRationale: Prevents the \\\"we didn't test for it, so we didn't find it\\\" loophole. Understanding what testing is and isn't being done is as important as knowing about incidents.\\n\\n**5. Include Close Calls and Capability Surprises**\\n\\nExplicitly include in reportable incidents:\\n- Unexpected capabilities that weren't designed or anticipated\\n- Near-misses where harm was narrowly avoided\\n- Behavior suggesting misalignment between model objectives and intended purpose\\n\\nRationale: These early warning signals are often more valuable than waiting for actual harm. Superintelligent AI may not give us second chances.\\n\\n**6. Build in Adaptive Evolution**\\n\\nMandate review and update of reporting requirements every 12 months.\\n\\nRationale: Our understanding of frontier AI risks is rapidly evolving. Reporting requirements must adapt.\\n\\n**7. Protect Good-Faith Reporting**\\n\\nCreate strong safe harbor protections for timely, thorough incident reporting. Penalties for concealment should be substantially higher than any penalties related to the incident itself.\\n\\nRationale: The incentive structure must strongly favor transparency.\\n\\n**8. Establish Independent Technical Review**\\n\\nCreate an independent technical review board to analyze serious incidents, publish findings, identify cross-cutting safety issues, and advise on updates to reporting requirements.\\n\\nRationale: Prevents regulatory capture and ensures technical expertise in incident analysis.\\n\\n### Critical Implementation Concerns\\n\\n**Regulatory Capacity**: Incident reporting is only valuable if the regulator can understand and act on reports. This requires sufficient technical expertise, clear escalation protocols, coordination mechanisms across agencies, and international information sharing.\\n\\n**Defining \\\"Frontier Model\\\"**: Consider capability-based thresholds, compute-based thresholds, and regular updates as state-of-the-art advances.\\n\\n**Open-Source Models**: Clarify how incident reporting applies to open-source frontier models.\\n\\n### Why This Matters Now\\n\\nAs AI capabilities rapidly advance, we are in a critical window for establishing safety norms and infrastructure. The quality of this reporting framework could determine whether we get advance warning of emerging risks or discover problems only after serious harm occurs.\\n\\n### Conclusion\\n\\nI strongly support this rulemaking and urge adoption of these improvements to maximize its safety value. The recommendations above would strengthen the rule by capturing the right information, enabling collective learning, creating accountability while maintaining appropriate incentives, and building in adaptation as our understanding evolves.\\n\\n---\\nFull technical analysis available at: https://halcyon-threshold.pagewell.app\\nContact: morgan@halcyonthreshold.org\"}"
